question.text: The footnote in Section 2.3.3 of Chapter 2 explains what 'leveraging at fund level' means for a Cat III hedge fund. Which of the following BEST captures why Chapter 2 singles out fund-level leverage as a defining risk of hedge funds, relative to other AIF categories?

answer.text: The fund borrows from market sources to make investments; debt must be repaid irrespective of investment gains or losses, magnifying both upside and downside risk
Fund-level leverage means investors individually borrow to buy units - the fund itself has no debt
Fund-level leverage is only notional and arises solely from unlisted PE co-investments
The leverage mechanism is simply a margin loan extended by the depositary with no recourse to the fund

explanation.text: The Logic: Footnote 7 in Section 2.3.3 (pp. 38, 254, 409) states: "Leveraging at fund level means that the fund entity will borrow from market sources in order to make investments as part of its investment activity. The idea is to generate arbitrage return for the fund by using debt (which costs lesser) to make investment gains (which are meant to be higher). However, this strategy also increases overall investment risk as the fund is obligated to pay back the debt irrespective of investment gains or losses." This is what separates hedge funds from other AIFs that do not leverage at fund level. The Trap: Option B inverts the concept - borrowing is at the FUND entity, not the investor. Option C reduces leverage to a PE co-invest artefact, which is wrong. Option D turns a meaningful regulatory and economic exposure into a settlement-margin detail. Note: The SEBI 2x leverage cap for Category III is computed using long plus short positions after permitted offsetting, per the workbook formula. Use that formula precisely when sizing positions rather than informal heuristics.
